\title{Measuring Complex Tastes: A Multiple Factor Analysis of Preferences, Consumption, and Evaluations in Musical Taste}

\author{Omar Lizardo\\ \small University of California, Los Angeles} \date{October 2026}

\begin{document}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
\noindent This paper develops a way to measure complex tastes---cases where what people like, do, and praise do not line up---using data that record preferences, engagement, and evaluations of the same objects, whether genre categories or specific cultural items. The approach applies Multiple Factor Analysis (MFA), a Geometric Data Analysis (GDA) method, and lets us ask concrete questions about complex tastes: Do preference, engagement, and evaluation contribute equally to the structure that emerges? Do some dimensions of complex taste hang together more than others? The method also captures a duality: individuals vary in how much their own tastes are complex, and genres vary in how much they attract complex tastes from the people who encounter them. I demonstrate the approach using data on Americans' tastes in twenty musical genres, collected around 2012.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

Sociologists have measured cultural taste in at least three different ways \citep{ma2026tastes}. One tradition treats taste as \emph{preference}: a person's affective response to a cultural object. A second treats it as an orientation toward \emph{consumption}: actual participation or engagement in a cultural field. A third treats it as a faculty expressed in \emph{valuation}: judgments about the quality or status of cultural objects. Rather than resolving this ambiguity by fiat, \citet{ma2026tastes} argues that taste should be understood pluralistically, as a person's ``thick subjectivity'' in a cultural field---a multidimensional orientation expressed through the multiple aspects of action that guide our preferences, engagement, and evaluations.

Taking taste's multiple aspects seriously sharpens the idea of \emph{complex taste}. In simple tastes, the aspects agree: what a person likes, does, and values all point the same way. In complex tastes they do not: the guilty pleasure (liked and consumed but not valued), the taste pose (liked and valued but not consumed), distanced consumption (consumed but neither liked nor valued), and their kin \citep{ma2026tastes}.

This paper takes that pluralist conception seriously and builds a measurement strategy to match. The strategy applies Multiple Factor Analysis (MFA) \citep{pages2014mfa,abdi2013mfa}---a member of the Geometric Data Analysis (GDA) family that \citet{bourdieu1984distinction} used in his classic study \citep{rouanet2000geometric-a44, roux2004geometric-65c}---to a data structure in which each cultural object is described by three sets of indicators, one per aspect of taste. MFA's block structure lets us ask the questions the theory raises directly: How strong are the links between preference, consumption, and evaluation? Do the three aspects contribute equally to the shared structure of taste? And where, geometrically, do complex tastes live?

\section{Data and Measures}

\subsection{Data}

I use the Survey Sample International (SSI) 2012 Cultural Tastes Survey \citep{lizardo2012ssi}, a national sample of $N = 2{,}276$ American adults surveyed around 2012. For each of twenty musical genres, the survey measures how much a respondent likes the genre, whether they consume it, and how they perceive the social characteristics of its typical fans. Listwise deletion of the $17$ cases missing data on any of the $60$ analysis variables leaves an analytic sample of $N = 2{,}259$ respondents.

\subsection{Measures: Three Aspects of Taste for Twenty Genres}

Each genre contributes three binary indicators, one per aspect, for $20 \times 3 = 60$ variables organized into three blocks of twenty. \textit{Preference} comes from a four-point liking scale (like; dislike; neither like nor dislike; not familiar); a genre is coded $1$ if the respondent likes it and $0$ otherwise, treating unfamiliarity as non-liking on the reasoning that an affective response requires knowing the object. \textit{Consumption} (engagement) is whether the respondent checked having listened to the genre in the past month ($1 = $ listened, $0 = $ otherwise). \textit{Evaluation} comes from a check-all-that-apply list of the social characteristics respondents attribute to a genre's ``typical fan,'' so the categories are not mutually exclusive---a respondent can indicate both that the typical fan is a college graduate and that they did not attend college, or that they are both working class and upper class. A genre is coded $1$ if the respondent attributed \emph{unambiguously} high status to its typical fans---a college graduate without also indicating no college, \emph{or} middle or upper class without also indicating working or lower class---and $0$ otherwise.

Table~\ref{tab:genre-rates} reports how often respondents are coded $1$ on each indicator. Overall, $41.7\%$ of genre-responses are positive on preference, $22.9\%$ on consumption, and $20.7\%$ on evaluation. The unambiguous-status standard is demanding---it requires an uncontested high-status signal in at least one domain---so evaluation is the least frequently affirmed aspect: respondents grant a genre's fans unambiguous high status less readily than they like the genre or listen to it.

\section{Analytic Strategy}

Our data gives us three separate pictures of each person's taste: what they like, what they listen to, and what they think about the people who do. These three pictures might overlap heavily (a person who likes opera probably listens to it and sees its fans as high status), or they might diverge sharply (someone might listen to hip-hop while considering it low status). We need a method that asks: How much do these three pictures agree? Do they contribute equally to a single coherent picture of musical taste? And where, geometrically, do people end up when their three pictures don't line up?

Multiple Factor Analysis (MFA) \citep{pages2014mfa,abdi2013mfa} is built precisely for this kind of problem. It takes data organized into distinct blocks of variables---here, the three aspects of taste---and builds a single shared picture of the people while making sure no one block dominates. The MFA literature calls these variable sets ``groups''; we use \emph{blocks of variables}, or \emph{aspects} when referring specifically to preference, engagement, and evaluation, reserving ``group'' for its ordinary sociological meaning. In the geometric data analysis tradition, the distinct values a variable can take (here yes/no) are called \emph{categories}. The MFA approach proceeds in two steps, which we describe in the following sections. 

\subsection{Constructing the Global Complex Taste Space}

The raw data is a table with one row per respondent and sixty columns: twenty genres, each measured on three aspects. Each entry is binary, containing a 1 if the person likes/listens to/evaluates the genre highly, and 0 otherwise. 

\emph{Step 1: Analyze each aspect separately.} We run a separate analysis on just the liking data (20 genres, 2,259 respondents), treating it as a two-way table of yes/no responses. This analysis shows how respondents cluster by what they like. We repeat the process independently for listening and for evaluations. In technical terms, each of these is a Multiple Correspondence Analysis (MCA) on one block of twenty binary variables. The result of each separate MCA is a map of the respondents, showing who is similar to whom in terms of liking alone, listening alone, or evaluations alone.

\emph{Step 2: Balance and combine.} After the first step, the next step is to merge these three separate pictures into one. But we face a problem here because if one aspect naturally has stronger patterns than another (if listening, say, reveals much sharper clustering than evaluations), it will dominate the combined picture. To prevent this, we weight each aspect inversely to the strength of the first dimension of the separate MCA we just described. The first MCA for preference had an eigenvalue of $0.200$; for consumption, $0.155$; for evaluation, $0.484$. The aspect with the largest eigenvalue has the strongest patterns, so we downweight it by using the weight $1/\lambda_1$: that gives weights of $5.00$ for preference ($1/0.200$), $6.45$ for consumption ($1/0.155$), and $4.28$ for evaluation ($1/0.484$). We apply these weights by multiplying all entries in each aspect-specific data table by the corresponding weight before combining them into the global analysis. The intuition is like handicapping in golf: the aspect with the strongest internal structure gets downweighted so all three contribute equally to the final picture. The result is the ``complex taste space''---a single map of respondents where all three aspects are heard equally.\footnote{As a robustness check, we re-estimated the same MFA with each block analyzed by scaled PCA instead of MCA; the results hold. Eigenvalues, RV coefficients, and individual coordinates correlate at $r > 0.96$ across the first three dimensions. The main difference is how rare categories are weighted: MCA emphasizes rare (distinctive) answers, a feature we want here since unusual taste patterns carry theoretical interest.}

\subsection{Independence or Redundancy of Aspects of Complex Tastes}

Before we interpret the combined space, we need to answer a basic question: \emph{Are the three aspects empirically separate, or are they measuring the same thing in three different ways?} If they're measuring the same underlying thing, we could just use preference and ignore the others. If they're distinct, complex tastes can exist---and do exist---because people will occupy different positions in preference space versus listening space versus evaluation space.

The \textit{RV coefficient} measures this. It answers: ``How similarly do two aspects rank respondents relative to each other?'' If two aspects rank people identically (so whoever likes the most genres also listens to the most, and evaluates the most highly), the RV is 1. If they rank people completely independently (knowing whether someone likes a lot tells you nothing about whether they listen a lot), the RV is 0. RV runs from 0 to 1, and it's the multivariate analog of a correlation coefficient between blocks of variables.\footnote{Formally, for each aspect $h$, the configuration matrix $\mathbf{S}_h$ captures pairwise respondent similarities based on that aspect's twenty variables. The RV coefficient between aspects $h$ and $k$ is the cosine of the angle between these two similarity structures: $\mathrm{RV}(h,k) = \mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{S}_h \mathbf{S}_k) / \sqrt{\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{S}_h^2)\,\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{S}_k^2)}$. When a block has a single variable, RV reduces to the squared Pearson correlation.}

If all three aspects were basically identical, we could measure complex tastes with just one. If they are distinct, people will occupy different positions when ranked by liking versus listening versus evaluations. This independence is the geometric signature of the complex-taste idea: the three aspects are distinct enough that a person can like a genre without listening, listen without liking, and evaluate highly without either. The section below shows whether this is actually the case empirically.

\subsection{Participation of Each Aspect in the Global Space}

We've established that the three aspects are partially independent. But when we combine them, do all three actually contribute to the final picture, or does one get washed out? The \textit{$Lg$ coefficient} answers this question. It measures: ``How much of each aspect's internal geometry survives in the combined picture?''

The $Lg$ coefficient tells us whether each aspect actually shows up in the combined picture. Because the balancing weights give each aspect equal influence going in, if an aspect ended up with a much weaker or stronger $Lg$, it would signal that aspect either didn't fit well with the others or dominated despite the handicap. The $Lg$ values are normalized so that, had each aspect shown up equally in the compromise, all three would have an $Lg$ of approximately $1$. The empirical results show whether all three aspects genuinely participate in the complex taste space.\footnote{Formally, $Lg(h, \mathrm{MFA})$ is the inner product of the configuration matrix for aspect $h$ with the configuration matrix of the combined MFA, on an absolute scale. The balancing weights ensure that each aspect's first axis contributes approximately equally to the global MFA in terms of inertia, so $Lg$ measures participation in the compromise as a whole.}

\subsection{Which Aspect Organizes Each Dimension?}

We know all three aspects participate in the space. But they don't participate equally on every dimension. The \textit{aspect contributions} answer: ``On this dimension, how much does each aspect contribute?''---that is, what share of the dimension's structure comes from each aspect? On Dimension 1, is the pattern mostly about liking? Mostly listening? Or a balanced mix?

Contributions sum to $100\%$ per dimension, so we can ask: Does one aspect dominate this dimension, or do all three push together? The dimensions that are dominated by a single aspect are exactly where the aspects can come apart most sharply, and where complex tastes should be most visible. The empirical results below show which dimensions are shared and which are aspect-specific.\footnote{The contribution of aspect $h$ to dimension $s$ is the sum of the squared coordinates of its twenty variables on that dimension, weighted and normalized by the dimension's overall variance.} 

\subsection{Measuring How Much Individual Tastes Come Apart}

So far we've asked about the space as a whole: How independent are the aspects? Do all three participate? Which aspect owns which dimension? Now we flip back to the individual level, asking: \emph{For each person, on each dimension, how much do their three aspects agree or disagree?}

\subsubsection{Agreement and Disagreement Between Aspects}

The technical machinery goes as follows. Each person has three separate coordinates on each Dimension---one based on their liking, one on their consumption, one on their evaluations---one per aspect. For Dimension 1, let us call these $F_{1,\text{p}}$, $F_{1,\text{c}}$, $F_{1,\text{e}}$. These three aspect-specific coordinates are called that person's three \emph{partial points} on the dimension. Their global position on that Dimension is the average of these three partial points. But the three might not be very close. Person A might have all three coordinates at $+2$ (perfect agreement). Person B might have coordinates at $+3$, $+1$, and $-1$ (strong disagreement).

We measure this disagreement with a score called $W_s(i)$. This score answers the question: ``How much do this person's three aspects disagree on this dimension?'' If all three dimension-specific scores are identical, $W_s(i) = 0$ (simple taste, complete agreement). If they're far apart, $W_s(i)$ is large (complex taste, substantial disagreement).

Mathematically, the following decomposition holds exactly:

\begin{equation}
\sum_{h=1}^{H} F_{sh}(i)^2 \;=\; H \cdot F_s(i)^2 \;+\;
\underbrace{\sum_{h=1}^{H} \left(F_{sh}(i) - F_s(i)\right)^2}_{W_s(i)},
\label{eq:decomp}
\end{equation}

Where $F_s(i)$ is the person's global position (where all three aspects place them), $W_s(i)$ is the disagreement score, and $H = 3$ the number of aspects being considered. The first term ($H \cdot F_s(i)^2$) measures the person's position on the dimension---how far they sit from the center; the second term ($W_s(i)$) measures how much that position varies depending on which aspect we look at. To see how much disagreement matters for a dimension as a whole, we sum these individual scores across all respondents: $\sum_i W_s(i)$ gives the total within-respondent disagreement on dimension $s$, and dividing by the total inertia on that dimension $\sum_i \sum_h F_{sh}(i)^2$ gives the proportion of the dimension's variance that stems from aspect disagreement versus the respondents' shared positions on the dimension.\footnote{Formally, the dimension-level disagreement share is $\sum_i W_s(i) / \sum_i \sum_h F_{sh}(i)^2$. The denominator follows from eq:decomp summed across all respondents: $\sum_i \sum_h F_{sh}(i)^2 = \sum_i H \cdot F_s(i)^2 + \sum_i W_s(i)$, so the disagreement share plus the position share sum to one.}

An example makes the decomposition easier to grasp (Figure~\ref{fig:worked-example}). Consider a respondent who likes fifteen of the twenty genres---from jazz, musicals, and classic rock/oldies to top 40 and contemporary rock---listens to nine of them, and credits the fans of eighteen genres with unambiguously high status (a somewhat ecunemical person). On the first (horizontal) dimension, the general-affirmation axis, all three aspect points sit on the same side of the origin---preference at $+3.53$, consumption at $+3.05$, evaluation at $+2.28$, around a global point of $+2.95$---so the aspects disagree only about \emph{how much} this respondent engages, and only modestly: $W_1 = 0.8$, or 3\% of the projected partial inertia. The third (vertical) dimension, the status-valuation axis, tells a different story. The preference and consumption points sit slightly on the withholding side of the origin ($-0.66$ and $-1.33$), while the evaluation point lies far out on the side anchored by the genre evaluations ($+13.12$), since as we have seen, this respondent grants high status to nearly every genre's fans, a generosity of valuation that far outruns both their liking and their listening. The global point is $+3.71$, and now the disagreement dwarfs the position: $W_3 = (-0.66 - 3.71)^2 + (-1.33 - 3.71)^2 + (13.12 - 3.71)^2 = 133.1$, or 76\% of the projected partial inertia---nearly everything that places this respondent on the status-valuation dimension is disagreement between aspects, not shared orientation.\footnote{In Ma's combinatorial terms (see Appendix~\ref{app:configurations}), the same respondent holds thirteen genres in complex configurations: one guilty pleasure, seven taste poses, four instances of distant praise, and one instance of distanced consumption.} The second dimension (right panel of Figure~\ref{fig:worked-example}) tells a third story for the same respondent: the preference point sits just on the popular side of the origin ($-0.89$), while consumption and evaluation sit on the highbrow side ($+1.74$ and $+4.31$), around a global point of $+1.72$, giving $W_2 = 13.5$---60\% of the projected partial inertia.\footnote{As the discrete complement to this geometric measure, each genre--respondent pair is classified into one of Ma's eight configurations from the binary triple of orientations (preference, consumption, evaluation): the simple taste $(+++)$, the simple non-taste $(---)$, and the six complex tastes (Appendix~\ref{app:configurations}).}

\subsubsection{Pairwise Disagreements and Sources of Complexity}

We can drill down further. The $W_s(i)$ score is made up of three pairwise disagreements: between liking and listening, between liking and evaluations, and between listening and evaluations. Each pairwise distance captures how far apart two aspects place a person on this dimension. The three pairwise distances sum exactly to $H \cdot W_s(i)$, so we can ask: ``Which pair of aspects is responsible for most of the disagreement on this dimension for each individual?'' On Dimension 3 (status), the preference--evaluation and consumption--evaluation distances will likely be large (evaluations place people far from where liking/listening do). On Dimension 1 (engagement), they might be more balanced.\footnote{The squared pairwise distance between aspects $h$ and $k$ is simply $(F_{sh}(i) - F_{sk}(i))^2$. The three distances sum exactly to $H \cdot W_s(i)$.}

Pairwise disagreements capture which aspects pull against each other, but they don't distinguish two very different mechanisms by which a person's taste becomes complex. A respondent might hold contradictory opinions of a single genre---liking it but not valuing it highly, for instance---or the same kind of disagreement might appear across multiple genres in a way that cancels out. We can decompose $W_s(i)$ to separate these two sources of disagreement.

\begin{equation}
W_s(i) \;=\; \underbrace{\sum_{g=1}^{G} \omega_s(i;g)}_{\text{genre-based}} \;+\; \underbrace{2H^2 \sum_{g < g'} \sum_{h=1}^{H} d_{ighs} d_{ig'hs}}_{\text{cross-genre coherence}}
\label{eq:genre}
\end{equation}

The first term, $\sum_g \omega_s(i;g)$, captures the respondent's \emph{genre-based complex taste}---how much the three aspects disagree within specific genres, summed across all twenty genres.\footnote{In Equation~\ref{eq:genre}, $\omega_s(i;g) = H^2 \sum_{h=1}^{H} d_{ighs}^2$, where $d_{ighs}$ is the deviation of aspect $h$'s partial coordinate from the respondent's genre-specific aspect average in genre $g$ on dimension $s$. The second term is the sum of pairwise cross-products of these deviations across all genre pairs $(g, g')$ and aspects $h$, weighted by $2H^2$. Positive coherence means per-genre disagreements reinforce; negative coherence means they cancel.} This component is large when a respondent's three aspects contradict each other within specific genres---when, for example, a person likes a genre but doesn't value it (a guilty pleasure), or values it without listening (distant praise). The second term represents \emph{cross-genre coherence}---the extent to which per-genre disagreements reinforce or cancel each other. Consider a respondent who likes jazz but not opera (preference disagreement within one genre pair) and listens to classical but not folk (consumption disagreement within another genre pair). If these two kinds of disagreement happen to offset each other when summed across all genres, the coherence term will be large and negative, reducing the total score. Conversely, if per-genre disagreements all push in the same direction---the same genres driving preference, consumption, and evaluation in different orders---the coherence term is large and positive, amplifying disagreement. A person with high coherence across genres shows a consistent pattern of contradiction; one with high genre-based disagreement shows conflicted taste in specific objects.

An example illuminates both components. Respondent 362 (discussed in detail below) has $W_3 = 133.1$ on the status-valuation dimension. This splits into $8.5$ from genre-based disagreement and $124.6$ from cross-genre coherence---94\% of the person's high score comes from having per-genre disagreements that reinforce each other rather than from holding contradictions within single genres. A person might instead have low total disagreement driven mostly by genre-local contradictions that happen to cancel; conversely, another might accumulate large total disagreement from small per-genre tilts that all point the same way. The two mechanisms have different meanings and, as the results below show, different social patterns.

\section{Results}

\subsection{Overall Structure of the Complex Taste Space}

How large and clear are the patterns in the complex taste space? Table~\ref{tab:eigen} shows that the first dimension captures $9.6\%$ of the variation, the second $7.5\%$, and the first five dimensions together $32.5\%$. These percentages are typical for data like ours---binary yes/no responses scattered across twenty genres analyzed via MCA. Much of the variation is genre-specific (whether you like opera has little to do with whether you like hip-hop), so no single dimension captures huge amounts. In the Geometric Data Analysis tradition, this variation is called \emph{inertia}---the total spread or dispersion of the respondent cloud around its center. When we say a dimension captures $9.6\%$ of the inertia, we mean that ordering respondents along that dimension explains $9.6\%$ of how different they are from one another.\footnote{We conducted all analyses in \textsf{R} using \textsf{FactoMineR}; scripts reproducing all results are available in the replication materials.}

The category coordinates reveal what each dimension means and they are shown in Figure~\ref{fig:categories1-2}. As we can see, on the first dimension, the pattern is simple and strong, with the yes categories of preference and consumption (especially the rarest ones---folk at $+1.43$, bluegrass at $+1.34$) sitting on the positive side and the no categories (unmarked gray points) sitting on the negative side. Status attributions barely move along this dimension (ranging from $+0.03$ for musicals to $+0.53$ for rap). So Dimension 1 is an \emph{engagement volume} dimension---where people sit depends on how many genres they like and listen to, regardless of what they think of the fans of each genre. Respondents who like and listen to many genres sit on the positive side. Those who like and listen to few sit on the negative side. Evaluations are nearly silent here.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=.85\linewidth]{fig-categories} \caption{Category map of the MFA (dimensions 1--2). Colored points are the ``yes'' categories of each aspect; grey points are the corresponding ``no'' categories. Preference and consumption ``yes'' categories array along the positive side of Dimension 1 (general affirmation); the evaluation ``yes'' categories barely spread along it, while splitting highbrow (top) from popular (bottom) on Dimension 2.}
\label{fig:categories1-2}
\end{figure}

Dimension 2 cuts across genres along a traditional hierarchical line based on ``brow'' status. The traditionally consecrated ``highbrow'' genres (opera, classical, big band, musicals) sit at the positive pole, while popular genres (rap, heavy metal, indie, dance/club, reggae) sit at the negative pole. Strikingly, this opposition shows up identically across all three aspects. Whether you measure liking, listening, or evaluations, the same genres cluster together. This is the classic \emph{highbrow--popular hierarchy} that researchers have documented for decades \citep{bourdieu1984distinction,jæger2024from-a4b}. Respondents move along this axis depending on where they fall in that genre hierarchy, and it is driven mainly by generation \citep{lizardo2015musical-8c6}, with older people tending toward highbrow (Section~\ref{sec:social}) and younger people toward popular.

The vertical axis of the category map in the right hand panel of Figure~\ref{fig:categories1-2} (Dimension 3) tells a different story. All twenty evaluation yes categories sit clustered on the positive side of the origin. The preference and consumption yes categories, by contrast, scatter around zero. On this dimension, the rarer the high-status attribution for a genre, the higher that genre sits---popular genres receive high-status attributions from fewer respondents, making their fans appear as distinctive high-status recipients. This is the \emph{status-valuation} dimension, almost entirely an evaluation axis. A respondent's position here depends almost solely on how they distribute status recognition across genres' fans, independent of their liking or listening. Generous respondents---those who grant high status to fans of most genres---sit high on the vertical axis, while respondents who reserve high status for traditionally consecrated genres (like classical or opera) sit low.

\subsection{Independence or Redundancy Among Complex Taste Aspects}

The Analytic Strategy section asked: Are the three aspects distinct or the same thing measured three ways? The RV coefficients answer the question empirically. Preference and consumption rank respondents quite similarly (RV = 0.32), but not identically. If you like a lot of genres, you probably listen to a lot too. But not everyone who listens a lot likes a lot, and vice versa---the two are far from perfectly correlated.

Evaluation, though, is a different story. It shows an RV of $0.01$ with both preference and consumption. This near-zero is the key empirical finding: evaluations rank respondents almost completely independently of their liking and listening. Knowing whether someone likes many genres tells you virtually nothing about whether they grant high status to genres' fans. The three aspects are genuinely distinct. What you like, what you listen to, and what you praise are three separable dimensions of taste. This is why complex tastes exist: a person can like a genre without listening to it, listen without liking, or evaluate highly without either liking or listening. None of these patterns is surprising or contradictory. They're the natural result of the three aspects being partially independent.

\subsection{How Each Aspect Participates in Each Dimension}

We've seen that all three aspects contribute to the global space, but they don't contribute equally to every dimension. On Dimension 1 (engagement volume), liking and listening align strongly (correlations $0.84$ and $0.86$ with the global axis), while evaluations barely correlate ($0.19$). On Dimension 2 (highbrow--popular), liking and listening again dominate and converge, with the genre hierarchy showing up consistently in both; evaluations contribute only modestly ($0.35$ correlation). Dimension 3, by contrast, is the evaluation-specific axis: it correlates almost perfectly with evaluation ($0.91$) and barely at all with preference and consumption ($< 0.15$). Respondents' liking and listening tell you almost nothing about where they sit on the status-valuation dimension---that's determined almost entirely by their evaluations.

\subsection{Which Aspect Dominates Each Dimension?}
\label{sec:contrib}

We've seen that dimensions 1 and 2 are shared across aspects, while dimension 3 is evaluation-dominated. But how dominant is each aspect on each dimension? On Dimension 1, is the split 50-50-0, or more balanced? We can answer this by looking at the aspect contributions---the percentage of each dimension's variation that comes from each aspect. Table~\ref{tab:groups} shows these percentages alongside the $Lg$ coefficients, which measure overall participation.

\label{tab:groups}

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering \caption{Partial axes: correlations between aspect-specific separate-analysis axes and the first three MFA dimensions.}
\label{tab:partial-axes}

\end{table}

The pattern is clear: Dimensions 1 and 2 are genuinely shared. Preference and consumption contribute roughly equally to both (around 48\% each on Dimension 1, 40--49\% on Dimension 2), while evaluation contributes modestly (2.5\% and 11\%). But Dimension 3 breaks the pattern entirely. Evaluation accounts for 83.9\% of it, while preference and consumption each contribute only 8\%. 

This reflects the fundamental structure of the space. Respondents' liking and listening reveal which rung of the genre hierarchy they occupy. But their evaluations reveal something else: how far down the hierarchy they're willing to extend recognition. The evaluation yes categories are ordered by rarity---granting status to rap fans is a distinctive move ($+1.87$), while granting it to opera fans is nearly universal ($+0.20$) and barely differentiates respondents at all. Dimension 3 is thus the evaluation-specific axis, where preference and consumption barely vary.

\subsection{Measuring Complex Tastes}
\label{sec:antinomies}

Now we get to the core question: \emph{For each person, on each dimension, how much do their three aspects disagree?} We measure this with the score $W_s(i)$ (Equation~\ref{eq:decomp}), the dispersion of a person's three partial coordinates around their global position. It's zero when all three aspects place them at the same location (simple taste) and grows as they place them further apart (complex taste).

What's surprising is how much complex tastes matter geometrically. On Dimension 1, the disagreement score accounts for 56\% of the total variation (inertia) on that dimension---meaning that 56\% of the variation comes from respondents' aspects disagreeing with each other, and 44\% comes from respondents' actual positions on the dimension (where the three aspects agree). On Dimension 2, it's 52\% disagreement versus 48\% position. On Dimension 3, it's 63\% disagreement versus 37\% position. This means aspect disagreement is nearly as important as respondents' positions in shaping the structure of the space. Complex tastes aren't a marginal phenomenon confined to a few unusual respondents. They're woven throughout the structure of the space.

We can also count complex tastes combinatorially: How many of a person's 20 genres fall into each of Ma's eight configurations? (Appendix~\ref{app:configurations} defines these.) The geometric and combinatorial measures are related but different. The geometric score on Dimension 1 correlates with the combinatorial count ($\rho = 0.31$), but on Dimensions 2 and 3 the correlation is much weaker ($0.19$ and $-0.06$). The reason: The geometric score measures \emph{how much} the aspects disagree on this dimension; the configuration count measures \emph{how many genres} a person holds in each configuration. They align on engagement (Dimension 1) but diverge on position (Dimension 2) and evaluation (Dimension 3).

Figure~\ref{fig:signatures} shows these geometric signatures: each of Ma's eight configurations occupies a distinct position in the space, mapping where different types of complex tastes cluster.

\subsection{The Social Sources of Complex Tastes}
\label{sec:social}

A key question: \emph{Is complex taste concentrated in certain demographic groups, or scattered across society?} While the distribution of taste positions across demographic groups is well-established, the social patterning of disagreement among aspects remains unexplored. Do some demographic groups experience more or less disagreement between what they like, listen to, and value?

\subsection{Who Has Complex Tastes?}
\label{sec:who}

We've shown that complex tastes are geometrically important and spread throughout the space. But are they concentrated in particular demographic groups? If younger people have more complex tastes, or if they're concentrated among the college-educated, that would matter for understanding the phenomenon.

The answer is surprising: \emph{they're scattered across all demographic groups}. When we regress each $W_s$ score on the eight demographic variables (age, education, income, race, class, gender, parents' education, and region), the results are telling: demographics explain only $5.2\%$ of the variation in $W_1$, $2.0\%$ in $W_2$, and $2.1\%$ in $W_3$. By contrast, where you sit in the space (your global position on each dimension) is strongly predicted by demographics ($\eta^2$ ranging from 0.03 to 0.33). You can predict fairly well whether someone likes highbrow or popular music based on their age and education \citep{lizardo2015musical-8c6}. But predicting how much their liking, listening, and evaluating disagree? Much harder. Complex tastes aren't the signature of any one social location.

The few effects that do appear are minor: upper-class respondents show slightly elevated disagreement on $W_1$ and $W_3$, those with college-educated parents score higher on $W_1$, and age matters slightly on $W_2$. If anything, complex tastes are slightly more common among the educated and affluent. But the overall pattern is clear: complex tastes are a general feature of individual taste profiles, not concentrated in any social group. The three aspects---liking, listening, evaluating---are weakly coupled for everyone, not just for certain demographic groups. The disagreement between them is as likely to appear among young people and working-class respondents as among older people and the college-educated.

This weak overall social patterning masks an important distinction. Recall that the disagreement score $W_s(i)$ decomposes into two components: the \emph{genre-based} part (how much a respondent's three aspects disagree within specific genres, denoted $\omega_s$) and the \emph{cross-genre coherence} part (how much per-genre disagreements reinforce or cancel across genres). These two mechanisms show strikingly different social patterns. The genre-based component is more socially structured: demographics explain $8.5\%$, $8.0\%$, and $3.3\%$ of its variation across the three dimensions (compared to $5.2\%$, $2.0\%$, and $2.1\%$ for the total scores). Upper-class respondents show elevated genre-based disagreement on all three dimensions, and parents' education predicts it on the first two. But the cross-genre coherence component---whether per-genre disagreements align or cancel---remains largely social-location-independent. What this suggests: while social position doesn't determine how much people disagree overall, it does shape \emph{which genres} anchor their complex tastes. The educated and affluent tend to hold complex tastes concentrated in specific genres (high $\omega$), whereas working-class respondents' complex tastes are more scattered across genres with offsetting disagreements (high coherence). Social location thus shapes the \emph{texture} of complex taste profiles without determining their overall magnitude.

\subsection{Which Genres Anchor Complex Tastes? Demographic Concentration}
\label{sec:genre-specificity}

Beyond the aggregate level, genre-specific disagreement reveals which demographic groups hold complex tastes concentrated in particular repertoires. The educated and affluent do not simply hold \emph{more} disagreement overall; they concentrate it in specific cultural objects---notably prestige genres like opera and classical music. Respondents whose parents hold college degrees show the strongest genre-specific disagreement in opera ($r = 0.15$ on Dimension 2, $r = 0.14$ on Dimension 1), followed by indie rock, classical, and Broadway/musicals. This pattern suggests that educational capital structures not just \emph{whether} one's aspects disagree, but \emph{where} that disagreement concentrates. Educated respondents navigate these prestige forms through contradictory positions: liking but not valuing, listening without granting high status, or valuing without regular engagement.

Subjective class position cuts a different path. Lower positions on the class scale show negative correlation with rap and hip-hop ($r = -0.13$), concentrating genre-specific disagreement there---these genres capture working-class guilty pleasures and distanced consumption, where respondents like rap but withhold status attribution, or listen while maintaining an ironic distance from the genre's valuations. Higher positions on the class scale show more disagreement in Broadway/musicals and big band ($r = 0.13$ and $r = 0.11$), genres the affluent are more likely to encounter and evaluate at a distance.

Age creates the sharpest genre-specific patterns. Younger respondents hold substantially more genre-specific disagreement in rap and hip-hop ($r = -0.43$), indie rock ($r = -0.34$), and dance/club music ($r = -0.24$)---the popular genres that define contemporary youth culture. Their disagreement reflects conflicted engagement: they may like these genres intensely but resist full identification with them, or listen widely while selectively evaluating. Older respondents, by contrast, concentrate disagreement in big band and jazz ($r = 0.19$ and modest positive effects), genres encountered less frequently and navigated with less fluency.

Gender differences emerge primarily in genres coded by masculine cultural expression. Respondents not identifying as women hold significantly more genre-specific disagreement in big band ($r = -0.12$) and heavy metal ($r = -0.10$)---both male-coded genres where complex configurations are more prevalent. Respondents identifying as women show concentrated disagreement in hymns and gospel ($r = 0.09$), suggesting navigation between personal liking and collective religious or cultural valuations.

Race and ethnicity show perhaps the clearest genre-specific patterns. Non-white respondents, especially Hispanic or Latino, concentrate genre-specific disagreement heavily in Latin/salsa music ($r = 0.31$ on Dimension 1, $r = 0.18$ on Dimension 2)---their own cultural form, navigated through complex relationships between personal liking, listening patterns, and broader status valuations. Rap and hip-hop show similar racialized disagreement ($r = 0.21$), as do dance and club music ($r = 0.20$ and $r = 0.15$). These genres cluster where cultural participation and evaluative distance intersect most acutely: respondents of color holding complex, often contradictory positions toward genres that represent both personal cultural identity and contested social status.

Figure~\ref{fig:omega-demographics} maps these patterns visually across eight demographically interesting genres. For continuous variables (age, parental education, gender), bars show correlations; for categorical variables (class and race), bars show each category's mean $\omega$ centered at the genre average, so positive values indicate above-average disagreement for that group and negative values indicate below-average. A blue bar means the demographic group or category holds \emph{more} genre-specific disagreement (their three aspects pull apart more); a red bar means \emph{less} disagreement (their responses cohere). For instance, the $r = -0.43$ correlation between age and $\omega$ for rap on Dimension 1 means older respondents have simpler, more unified positions on rap, while younger respondents show more contradictory responses---they may like rap intensely yet withhold listening, or listen widely yet selectively evaluate, creating the disagreement that the score captures. Among race categories, Black respondents show above-average disagreement in rap and hip-hop on Dimension 2 (mean difference $+0.24$), navigating this genre through multiple contradictory positions. The genre-based component thus becomes a window onto how demographic position shapes not just taste position but taste \emph{structure}---the specific locations where respondents experience their aspects pulling apart. Social location does not uniformly inflate disagreement; it localizes it, channeling complex tastes through particular cultural objects that carry demographic and social meaning.

\subsection{The Duality: Genres as Targets of Complex Tastes}
\label{sec:duality}

Complex tastes have a dual structure: individuals are \emph{sources} of complex tastes, and genres are \emph{targets}. Which genres attract complex tastes? Genres differ dramatically in how unified responses are.\footnote{At the genre level, we measure the proportion of respondents with simple tastes: those whose three aspects all agree (either all yes---like, listen, grant status---or all no). The complement is the proportion with complex tastes in that genre (any mismatch across aspects).} Heavy metal, Latin/salsa, and bluegrass elicit largely simple tastes: $70\%$, $67\%$, and $65\%$ of respondents show alignment across all three aspects. Classical and opera, by contrast, split audiences: only $33\%$ and $24\%$ of respondents have simple tastes in these genres. These prestige genres attract complex configurations---people who like but don't listen, listen but don't grant status, or value highly without engagement.

To answer this, we need a different analysis. The first MFA treated respondents as the units being analyzed and genres as variables. Now we flip that: rows become genres and columns become respondent-responses (each respondent's yes/no on liking, listening, and evaluation for each genre). We re-run the MFA with genres as units. This is not simply a rearrangement of the original solution; it is a fundamentally different analysis that asks new questions. In the original analysis, genres appeared only as variables; we could locate them through the composition of their audiences---the average profile of people who affirm them. But we cannot compute aspect-level agreement from the respondent analysis alone. Specifically, we cannot ask whether genres that are \emph{liked by many} are also \emph{listened to by many}---that is, whether the liking and listening audiences for each genre overlap. We also cannot see whether different aspects place individual genres in different positions. Both questions require treating genres as the units of analysis and respondents as the indicators.

Technically, this flip changes the analysis fundamentally. Because MFA weights each block inversely to its separate analysis's strength, and transposing reshuffles which variables define the blocks, the balancing weights change: the transposed separate analyses yield different first eigenvalues ($\lambda_1' = 1.95/1.48/1.05$ for preference/consumption/evaluation respondent-indicators, versus the original $0.200/0.155/0.484$ for genre-indicators). The transposed dimensions are thus optimized for spreading genres apart, not respondents. The key statistics we want---RV coefficients comparing aspects at the genre level, and aspect-specific partial points showing where different respondent-groups place each genre---do not exist in the respondent-level fit. The transposed MFA was implemented by direct application of the algorithm in \citet{pages2014mfa} and validated by reproducing the respondent-level \textsf{FactoMineR} solution: eigenvalues, global and partial coordinates, RV coefficients, and group contributions all agree to within $10^{-4}$. Dropping respondents with constant values (always like/listen/evaluate or never do so across all genres), we exclude $83$, $84$, and $326$ respondent-variables respectively.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig-genre-map} \caption{Genre map from the transposed MFA. Black points: genre compromise positions; colored points: aspect partial points (segments connect each genre's compromise to its aspect-specific positions).}
\label{fig:genre-map}
\end{figure}

Here's the surprise: From the genre perspective, the aspects \emph{agree} strongly. The RV coefficients are $0.92$ (preference--consumption agree), $0.53$ (preference--evaluation), and $0.49$ (consumption--evaluation)---far higher than the individual-level $0.32$, $0.01$, and $0.01$. People who like a genre tend to listen to it and grant its fans status. But this doesn't contradict our individual-level findings. The agreement is \emph{at the aggregate level} (recall the classic ecological fallacy). Yes, the liking population and the listening population overlap substantially for each genre. But \emph{which individuals} occupy which positions varies. Complex tastes aren't a property of genres; they're a property of individuals. One person's complex taste is another person's simple taste.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering \caption{Genre target profiles: percentage of respondents holding each genre in each of Ma's configurations ($N = 2{,}259$).}
\label{tab:genre-profile}
\input{tables/tab-genre-profile}
\end{table}

The transposed space is itself strongly structured ($\lambda_1 = 2.27$, $14.6\%$ of the inertia; $\lambda_2 = 1.95$, $12.5\%$). Its second dimension is a \emph{configuration axis}: genres are ordered by the complex-taste profiles they attract (Table~\ref{tab:genre-profile}). At the positive pole sit the genres respondents actively hold---in simple positive taste ($\rho = +0.77$), as taste poses ($+0.55$), as guilty pleasures ($+0.44$), or as justified abstentions ($+0.44$)---led by classic rock/oldies ($+3.7$), mood/easy listening ($+2.0$), country ($+1.8$), and top 40/pop ($+1.3$). At the negative pole sit genres whose dominant relation is simple non-taste ($\rho = -0.73$): rap/hip-hop ($-1.7$), reggae ($-1.5$), latin/Spanish/salsa ($-1.3$), and heavy metal ($-1.3$)---together with opera ($-1.2$), whose relation to its audience is instead dominated by distant praise ($58.9\%$ of respondents hold it in that configuration). The duality is asymmetric in exactly the way complex-taste theory anticipates: the prototypical guilty-pleasure genres are among the least credited with high status (evaluation rates of $8$--$14\%$ for classic rock/oldies, country, and top 40), and the prototypical distant-praise genre is the least consumed ($8.5\%$ for opera). The first dimension opposes genres whose typical relation is status without engagement---classical ($-3.6$), opera ($-3.0$), and musicals ($-2.1$), with distant-praise rates loading at $-0.82$ and taste-pose rates at $-0.58$---against genres held in guilty pleasure ($\rho = +0.75$) and distanced consumption ($+0.80$): top 40 ($+2.0$), rap/hip-hop ($+1.8$), classic rock/oldies ($+1.3$), and contemporary rock ($+1.3$)---familiar genres most often held with engaged disagreement.

Finally, the partial points show where the aspects disagree about specific objects despite their overall agreement. On the third dimension, the evaluation partial points of consecrated genres sit displaced toward positive values relative to their preference and consumption partial points (classical: $+2.3$ for evaluation against $+1.0$ for preference and $+0.9$ for consumption; opera: $+2.3$ against $-0.0$ and $+0.1$), while country shows the reverse displacement (evaluation $-0.8$ against $-3.1$ and $-4.1$). Status attributions, in other words, are distributed across genres in a way that only partially tracks who likes and who listens---echoing, at the level of objects, the aspect independence we already established at the level of sources.

\section{Discussion}

This paper has pursued a geometric approach to measuring complex tastes---the misalignments between preference, consumption, and evaluation in cultural fields. The results support three core findings about musical taste in contemporary America.

\emph{First, the three aspects are empirically independent.} Preference and consumption correlate moderately (RV = 0.32), but evaluation is nearly orthogonal to both (RV = 0.01). This independence is the geometric signature of the complex-taste concept. If all three were measuring the same underlying thing, we could ignore two of them. But they don't. What you like, what you listen to, and what you praise are three separable judgments that follow different logics.

\emph{Second, the shared structure is primarily two-dimensional.} The first dimension is engagement volume: how many genres someone likes and listens to. The second is the classical highbrow--popular hierarchy. Both dimensions are visible across all three aspects, reflecting shared cultural structures that shape how people organize musical taste. Evaluations are largely silent on these dimensions, appearing only modestly on the first and second, but dominating a distinct third dimension.

\emph{Third, complex tastes are ubiquitous.} The disagreement scores ($W_s$) account for $56\%$, $52\%$, and $63\%$ of variation on the three dimensions. Combinatorially, the average respondent holds $10.2$ of $20$ genres in complex configurations. Only 12 respondents (of 2,259) hold no complex configuration at all. This is not a marginal phenomenon. Complex tastes are woven throughout the taste landscape.

A surprising finding follows: complex tastes are not concentrated in any social group. Where respondents sit (whether they prefer highbrow or popular genres) is strongly predicted by age, education, and class. But how much their three aspects disagree is nearly unpredictable from demographics. The dispersion that makes a person's taste complex is orthogonal to the social positions that sort people by consumption patterns. This fits the individual-level theory. The independence of the aspects at the population level generates disagreement at the individual level whenever people don't occupy all three positions simultaneously.

Finally, the duality reveals something crucial: from the genre perspective, the aspects agree. Liking, listening, and evaluation audiences overlap substantially. But because individuals don't equally participate in all three audiences, complex tastes emerge. A person may be a genuine opera enthusiast (likes, listens, praises) or a genuinely uninterested person (none of the above) or any combination. The eight configurations are not rare types; they're how ordinary people relate to culture when three incompletely correlated judgment systems structure their engagement.

Future work might explore whether these patterns generalize to other cultural fields---visual art, film, fashion---or whether music has distinctive properties. The geometric approach makes possible precise measurement of the degree to which cultural judgment is unified or fragmented. The results here suggest it's fundamentally fragmented.

\appendix

\section{The Combinatorial Measure: Ma's Eight Configurations}
\label{app:configurations}

The geometric measure locates complex tastes continuously in the common space. As a discrete complement, each genre--respondent pair can be classified into one of Ma's eight configurations from the binary triple of orientations (preference, consumption, evaluation): the simple taste $(+++)$, the simple non-taste $(---)$, and the six complex configurations.

Complex tastes are the statistical norm of this taste culture, not the exception. Figure~\ref{fig:configurations} reports the mean number of genres held in each configuration: the average respondent holds $10.2$ of the $20$ genres in a complex configuration, and only $12$ of $2{,}259$ respondents hold no complex configuration at all. The most frequent complex configuration is the \emph{justified abstention} ($3.3$ genres on average), followed by the \emph{guilty pleasure} ($3.2$) and \emph{distant praise} ($2.2$): respondents routinely like genres whose fans they don't credit with high status, grant high status to genres they neither like nor consume, and like-and-consume genres whose fans they don't credit that way. The taste pose ($1.0$) and the rare variants---distanced consumption ($0.4$) and the pre-acquired taste ($0.1$)---are comparatively infrequent, while the simple non-taste ($8.9$) is the single largest configuration.
